name: Nature trivia (easy)
description: 50 easy questions about animals, plants, weather, ecosystems. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Which animal is the largest on Earth?
items.explain: The blue whale is the largest animal on Earth. It is also the largest animal known ever to have lived.

items.question: What do blue whales feed on almost exclusively?
items.explain: Blue whales strain huge volumes of ocean water through their baleen plates to catch krill, and they eat almost nothing else.

items.question: To which animal group do blue whales belong?
items.explain: The blue whale is a marine mammal.

items.question: Which gas do plants take in from the air to carry out photosynthesis?
items.explain: Plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make sugar and oxygen.

items.question: Which gas do green plants release as a by-product of photosynthesis?
items.explain: In photosynthesis, green plants turn light energy, water and carbon dioxide into energy-rich compounds and release oxygen.

items.question: What is the name of the green pigment in plants that helps them make food from sunlight?
items.explain: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in plants that perform photosynthesis.

items.question: Through which part of a tree is water mainly taken up from the soil?
items.explain: Tree and plant roots absorb water, minerals and nutrients from the soil, while the leaves absorb carbon dioxide from the air.

items.question: Which energy source do plants use to make their own food through photosynthesis?
items.explain: Plants need carbon dioxide, water and light energy from the Sun to make sugar and oxygen.

items.question: Which animal is the fastest on land?
items.explain: The cheetah is the world's fastest land mammal, able to go from zero to 60 miles an hour in about three seconds.

items.question: What does a cheetah's light tail help it do during a high-speed chase?
items.explain: A cheetah's light tail acts like a rudder, helping it stay stable and turn quickly while chasing prey.

items.question: Which animal is the tallest on land?
items.explain: Giraffes are the tallest land animals. Males can top 5.5 metres (18 feet).

items.question: Giraffes feed mostly on the leaves of which kind of tree?
items.explain: Giraffes feed mostly on acacia leaves, stripping them from branches with their long prehensile tongues.

items.question: On which continent do wild giraffes live?
items.explain: Giraffes live in habitats across Africa, from savannahs to woodlands.

items.question: What sweet liquid do bees search for when they visit flowers?
items.explain: Bees fly from plant to plant looking for nectar, the sweet liquid that flowers secrete.

source.title: Bees pollinate amid search for flowers' nectar

items.question: What is the name of the process in which bees carry pollen between flowers, helping plants reproduce?
items.explain: Bees collect pollen on their bodies and leave it on the next flower they visit, which pollinates the plant.

source.title: Bees pollinate amid search for flowers' nectar

items.question: Which is the largest tropical rainforest in the world?
items.explain: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, covering over 5.5 million square kilometres in South America.

items.question: Which country contains the largest share of the Amazon rainforest?
items.explain: About 60% of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil, followed by Peru and Colombia.

items.question: Which activity has led to large areas of the Amazon rainforest being felled or burned?
items.explain: Large parts of the Amazon have been felled or burned to make way for cattle ranches and other activities.

source.title: The Amazon rainforest: The wonders of Earth's most unexplored wilderness, explained - BBC Science Focus Magazine

items.question: What is the calm region at the center of a hurricane called?
items.explain: The eye is a region of mostly calm weather at the center of a strong tropical cyclone.

items.question: Which part of a hurricane, ringing the eye, contains the storm's strongest winds?
items.explain: The eyewall surrounds the calm eye and holds the storm's strongest winds.

items.question: What causes the sound of thunder?
answers: Storm clouds smashing into each other
Air rapidly expanding around a lightning bolt
items.correct: Air rapidly expanding around a lightning bolt
items.explain: Lightning heats the air in its path so fast that it expands and creates a shock wave, which we hear as thunder.

items.question: Why do we usually see a lightning flash before we hear its thunder?
answers: Clouds hold back sound for a while
Light travels much faster than sound
Thunder forms only after rain begins
items.correct: Light travels much faster than sound
items.explain: Lightning is seen first because the speed of sound in air is much slower than the speed of light.

items.question: Roughly how many seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder equal a distance of one mile?
items.explain: Every five seconds between flash and thunder corresponds to about one mile, or three seconds per kilometre.

items.question: Which American is credited with discovering in 1752 that lightning is caused by electrical discharges?
items.explain: Benjamin Franklin showed as early as 1752 that lightning is a powerful electrical discharge.

items.question: Which kind of object does lightning usually strike?
items.explain: Lightning usually strikes the tallest object, which is why open fields and tall trees are dangerous in storms.

items.question: What is the aquatic larval stage of a frog called?
items.explain: A tadpole is the aquatic larval stage of frogs and toads.

items.question: Which organs do newly hatched tadpoles use to breathe underwater?
items.explain: Most tadpoles hatch as fully aquatic larvae that breathe through gills and swim with a long tail.

source.title: Interactive: Frog life cycle, from egg to adult - The Australian Museum

items.question: Where do most frogs lay their jelly-like eggs?
items.explain: Frogs lay jelly-like eggs in water, and these hatch into tadpoles.

source.title: The Frog Life Cycle for Kids - National Geographic Kids

items.question: What is the process called by which a caterpillar changes into a butterfly?
items.explain: The cycle from egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly is called metamorphosis.

items.question: What is the stage called in which a butterfly caterpillar changes into an adult?
items.explain: When a caterpillar reaches full size it forms a chrysalis (or pupa), and the adult butterfly develops inside.

items.question: What does a caterpillar spend most of its time doing?
items.explain: A caterpillar spends most of its time eating, until hormonal changes make it stop feeding and begin its transformation.

source.title: What Happens Inside The Chrysalis Of A Butterfly? - Sciencing

items.question: What is a baby kangaroo called?
items.explain: A baby kangaroo is called a joey. It is born tiny and underdeveloped and grows mostly inside its mother's pouch.

source.title: Story: 5 Facts About Kangaroo Joeys At Brookfield Zoo Chicago

items.question: Kangaroos belong to which group of mammals, named from a Latin word for "pouch"?
items.explain: The name marsupial comes from the Latin marsupium, meaning pouch. Kangaroos are marsupials.

items.question: At birth, a baby kangaroo is about the size of which object?
items.explain: A newborn joey is about jelly-bean sized and weighs less than a gram, so it finishes developing in the pouch.

source.title: What Is Inside a Kangaroo Pouch? - A-Z Animals

items.question: Which mammal is capable of true, powered flight?
items.explain: Bats are the only mammals capable of true powered flight. Animals like sugar gliders and flying squirrels only glide.

source.title: What Factors Shape the Flyability in Bats?—The Perspective from Bat's Wing Development - PMC

items.question: Bats are found on every continent except which one?
items.explain: Bats are remarkably adaptable and live on every continent except Antarctica.

items.question: Many bats find prey in the dark by using sound waves. What is this ability called?
items.explain: Many bats hunt in the dark by using sound waves, a skill known as echolocation.

items.question: Which prey do many bats eat in huge numbers, helping control pests such as mosquitoes?
items.explain: Many bats prey on insects, including agricultural pests and disease-carrying mosquitoes.

items.question: In what position do bats typically sleep?
items.explain: Bats are well known for sleeping upside down.

items.question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
items.explain: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and one pumps it to the rest of the body.

source.title: How Many Hearts Does an Octopus Have?

items.question: What color is an octopus's blood?
items.explain: Octopus blood is blue because the oxygen-carrying protein haemocyanin contains copper rather than iron.

source.title: Octopuses keep surprising us - here are eight examples how

items.question: How many arms does an octopus have?
items.explain: An octopus has an eight-armed body.

source.title: How Many Hearts Does an Octopus Have?

items.question: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
items.explain: At about 9.4 million square kilometers, the Sahara in northern Africa is the largest hot desert on Earth.

source.title: Not all Deserts are Sandy - National Geographic Education

items.question: What is a fertile spot in a desert, where underground water reaches the surface, called?
items.explain: In some places in the Sahara there is underground water. These places are called oases, and the water comes up through springs.

items.question: The name "Sahara" comes from an Arabic word meaning what?
items.explain: The name of the Sahara comes from the Arabic word for "desert".

source.title: The Sahara: Earth's largest hot desert

items.question: What kind of living things are corals?
items.explain: Corals may look like colorful rocks or plants, but they are animals that form colonies of tiny polyps.

items.question: What is the term for stressed corals losing their algae and turning white?
items.explain: When coral polyps are stressed by pollution or water that is too warm, they release their algae, which is called coral bleaching.

items.question: Coral reefs get their bright colors mainly from which living things in the coral's tissues?
items.explain: Coral reefs get their bright colors from algae called zooxanthellae that live in the coral's tissues.

items.question: Coral polyps are close relatives of which sea animals?
items.explain: Coral polyps are small, soft animals related to jellyfish and sea anemones.
